Car NCPs with G-EVs to combat and reverse AMR in Gram-negative pathogens. Our
comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that this innovative system achieves
remarkable antibacterial efficacy through collaborative enhancement mechanisms via
the depletion of intracellular ATP and disruption of efflux pump activity. Meanwhile,
targeted delivery approach of G-EVs with the combination of high drug loading
capacity and pH-triggered release behavior of Ce-Car NCPs, can significantly enhance
intracellular antibiotic accumulation and antibacterial efficacy (Fig. 3). Encouraged
by these in vitro favorable properties, the therapeutic efficacy of our platform is further
unequivocally demonstrated in a mouse model of drug-resistant P. aeruginosa
pneumonia. The treatment of Ce-Car@EV NPs significantly improves survival rates
and reduces bacterial loads not only in the lungs but also in other major organs (Fig.
6), including the heart, liver, spleen, and kidney (Supplementary Fig. 22-23). These
compelling in vivo antibacterial results, combined with the excellent biocompatibility
profile in safety assessments, strongly support the clinical potential of this
nanoplatform.
The strategic design of our platform builds upon yet substantially extends previous work
on both plant-derived vesicles and metal-drug coordination systems. While previous
studies have established the fundamental drug delivery capabilities of G-EVs,27, 44, 50
our research demonstrates their capacity to effectively and target-deliver sophisticated
metal-antibiotic coordination polymers while maintaining their innate biological
functions. This design represents a distinct advance beyond systems relying on external
energy, which directly targets the core physiological basis of resistance through energy
disruption and pathway interdiction. Crucially, the biomimetic properties of G-EVs
coating have been found to confer superior targeting capability intrinsically depending
on the pathological inflammatory microenvironment, as confirmed by our in vivo
biodistribution studies (Fig. 5). Furthermore, this rational integration predicts a
meaningful advancement over the conventional nanocarrier systems, as it not only
preserves the structural integrity of both components but also ensures a high local
concentration of therapeutic agents precisely at the desired site, thereby enhancing
antibacterial efficacy. Beyond their established role as delivery vehicles, the
immunomodulatory potential of G-EVs adds another dimension to our platform’s
therapeutic profile. Although a detailed investigation of immune modulation is beyond
the scope of this study, the emerging observations suggest that plant-derived vesicles
can interact with immune cells and modulate inflammatory responses,48, 51 thereby
extending their potential in clinical practices. This characteristic, combined with the
excellent antibacterial activity of our platform, provides a comprehensive approach to
infection management, which warrants further exploration in future studies.
The antibacterial effectiveness of Ce-Car@EV NPs against diverse Gram-negative
pathogens, including both P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae, stems from its unique
dual-mechanism approach. Both pathogens possess penicillin-binding proteins, which
serve as targets for carbenicillin’s inhibition of cell wall biosynthesis. Consequently,
Ce(IV) ions concurrently induce energy deprivation through ATP hydrolysis and
dissipation of the proton motive force (Fig. 4h-l). Overall, this coordinated attack on
structural integrity and energy metabolism enables effective suppression of diverse
resistant pathogens. Although our results are compelling, several frontiers remain to be
explored. The relative contribution of each targeting mechanism (e.g., passive EPR
effect vs. active biomimetic homing) warrants further deconvolution through more
sophisticated disease models. Additionally, the immunomodulatory potential of G-EVs
and a comprehensive investigation into their interaction with host immune cells may
reveal their powerful adjuvant effects, which can transform our nanoplatform from a
mere bactericidal agent into an immunotherapeutic one. In conclusion, the Ce-
Car@EV platform-mediated AMR antibacterial therapy presents a promising strategy
through the intelligent and rational integration of natural biostructures and synthetic
materials. This capability to simultaneously disrupt energy metabolism, inhibit efflux
pumps, and enable targeted delivery of agents allows it to effectively reverse bacterial
resistance and kill the AMR pathogenic bacteria, offering a promising avenue to combat
multidrug-resistant bacterial infections in clinics.” (Manuscript Page 25-27, Lines

suggests that the metabolic integrity and ATP-generating capacity of immune cells are
not compromised. Coupled with the pharmacokinetic data showing the rapid systemic
clearance of cerium, the release of cerium ions in an acidic infectious microenvironment

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The emergence of antimicrobial resistance is a critical global health challenge that renders conventional antibiotics ineffective. Developing innovative strategies to resensitize drug-resistant pathogens to existing antibiotics represents a promising therapeutic approach. Here, we present a biomimetic nanoplatform (Ce-Car@EVNPs) through the rational integration of ginger-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) and a pH-responsive cerium-carbenicillin coordination nanoparticles (Ce-CarNCPs). This design enables prolonged circulation and targeted degradation in acidic infection sites, releasing Ce4+ ions and carbenicillin. The released Ce4+ ions penetrate the bacterial cells, where they disrupt ATP synthesis, impede oxidative phosphorylation, and inhibit the activity of efflux pump. By depleting ATP, blocking efflux pumps, and thereby reversing bacterial resistance, Ce4+ ions act as a potent adjuvant to carbenicillin. Here we show that this strategy effectively restores carbenicillin efficacy against drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa both in vitro and in vivo, establishing a therapeutic strategy leveraging metallic adjuvants to counteract antimicrobial resistance.

---

## Introduction

Infections caused by pathogenic bacteria can result in various diseases including pulmonary infections, septic wounds, sepsis, and bacterial meningitis, posing a severe threat to global health1–4. Although antibiotics-mediated therapeutic strategies are regarded as the standard treatment for bacterial infections, their overuse and misuse have accelerated the development of antimicrobial resistant (AMR) bacterial strains, particularly in Gram-negative bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa), a high-priority pathogen known for its intrinsic resistance mechanisms5. Typically, P. aeruginosa is the leading pathogenic bacteria of respiratory infections, especially in immunocompromised individuals, such as cystic fibrosis patients, which ranks among the top respiratory pathogens in clinical settings according to the 2022 CHINET report6,7. Current treatments for P. aeruginosa infection rely on β-lactams, aminoglycosides, and fluoroquinolones8. However, the low outer membrane permeability and high efflux pump expression of pathogens contribute to both intrinsic and acquired resistance, resulting in the impairment of their therapeutic efficacy9. Notably, little progress in developing new antibiotics targeting Gram-negative bacteria has been made since the 1980s10, thus emphasizing the urgent need for optimized strategies to improve the clinical efficacy of existing antibiotics.

As the universal energy currency of bacteria, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) serves as the most immediate energy source for essential cellular functions, including DNA replication, protein synthesis, and active transport11. Importantly, ATP plays a dual pivotal role in bacterial antibiotic resistance, acting as both the core energy currency driving drug efflux via efflux pumps and a key signaling molecule regulating the expression of resistance genes12,13. This mechanistic insight reveals a promising therapeutic opportunity by achieving targeted depletion of intracellular ATP through an energy deprivation strategy, which can simultaneously inhibit efflux pump function and disrupt the resistance gene network, thereby resensitizing drug-resistant pathogens to conventional antibiotics and reversing bacterial resistance. Recent research has verified that cerium, a redox-active lanthanide metal, exhibits phosphatase-mimicking activity due to its multivalent states, demonstrating the capacity to selectively hydrolyze ATP and ADP14,15. This unique property enables the design of cerium-based nanoplatforms to effectively deplete intracellular ATP, providing potent energy-deprivation antibacterial strategies.

Although metal-based antimicrobial agents have broad-spectrum targeting capacity, their potential cytotoxicity has limited their development and clinical applications16. On the other hand, combining metal-based agents with conventional antibiotics offers a promising strategy to overcome the potential toxicity of metal compounds when treating drug-resistant bacterial infections17,18. For example, an orally administered bismuth compound in combination with N-acetylcysteine is currently undergoing phase II/III clinical trials as part of an anti-coronavirus cocktail therapy19. However, there are still many challenges in achieving optimal drug loading efficiency and precisely controlled release for targeted delivery. In this context, nanotechnology-based drug delivery strategies emerge as a promising solution to address these limitations. In particular, nanoscale coordination polymers (NCPs), consisting of metal ions and organic linkers, have gained attention as versatile delivery carriers due to their high porosity, tunable architecture, and structural flexibility20–22. Metal-drug coordination nanoplatform using drug as the organic linkers with the capacity to respond to weak acidic microenvironment provides a valuable opportunity for antibacterial applications, showing the efficient drug loading and controlled release23–25. Generally, nanoparticle clearance by the mononuclear phagocytic system limits drug delivery efficiency to infection sites26. Recently, biomimetic extracellular vesicle (EV)-coated nanoplatforms have received significant attention. Based on our previous finding that ginger-derived EVs enhance nanoparticle circulation and bacterial uptake27, we developed a pH-responsive Ce-Car@EV nanoplatform that combines high drug-loading metal-organic coordination polymers (NCPs) with EV-based immune evasion.

---

## Results

Preparation and characterization of Ce-Car@EV nanoplatforms
Car is a typical β-lactam antibiotic, whose two carboxyl groups can coordinate with various metal ions28. Hence, Car was utilized as organic bridge to connect with Ce(IV) ions for the construction of Ce-Car coordination polymers (Ce-Car NCPs) via a one-pot self-assembly of Ce(IV) and Car through coordination interactions (Fig. 2a). Ginger-derived EVs (G-EVs) were extracted via differential and density gradient centrifugation, subsequently encapsulating Ce-Car NCPs under the treatment of ultrasonication to form Ce-Car@EV nanoparticles (Ce-Car@EV NPs) (Fig. 2a). As shown in Fig. 2b, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images reveal that Ce-Car NCPs exhibited a homogeneous spherical structure with an average diameter of about 10 nm, while EVs displayed a typical saucer-like shape. Notably, TEM images of Ce-Car@EV NPs show that Ce-Car NCPs were primarily encapsulated within G-EVs, confirming the successful preparation of the Ce-Car@EV hybrid nanoplatform. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis verified the presence of distinct Ce 3d, O 1s, and N 1s peaks in the structure of Ce-Car@EV NPs (Supplementary Fig. 1), while the high-resolution XPS spectra revealed the presence of both Ce(IV) and Ce(III) species at a ratio of 71.5:28.5 (Supplementary Fig. 2). Various studies have shown that the ligand-to-metal or metal-to-ligand charge transfer processes may occur in metal complexes, and smaller energy gaps usually indicate that charge transfer is more likely to occur within the complex molecule29. According to the simulation results, the energy gap between HOMO (the highest occupied molecular orbital) and LUMO (the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital) of Ce-Car NCPs is 1.393 eV, indicating that Ce(IV) is successfully coordinated to Car, and the charge transfer can occur between the metal node and organic ligand (Fig. 2c). In addition, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy provides additional evidence for the successful formation of Ce–O bonds between Ce(IV) and Car in the coordination structure of Ce-Car NCPs (Fig. 2d). The hydrodynamic size distribution assessed by dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis showed a profile consistent with the TEM findings (Supplementary Fig. 3). The zeta potential of Ce-Car NCPs decreased from approximately −2.6 to −16.2 mV upon the encapsulation of G-EVs, further confirming the successful construction of Ce-Car@EV NPs (Fig. 2e). Additionally, sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) analysis reveals that the resultant Ce-Car@EV NPs retained the surface proteins of biologically active G-EVs (Fig. 2g). Furthermore, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 4, Western blot image indicates that the exosomal marker protein CD9 is present on Ce-Car@EVs NPs, which are broadly consistent with SDS-PAGE findings. Therefore, these results demonstrate the successful synthesis of Ce-Car NCPs and G-EVs coating of Ce-Car@EV NPs.

As the important component of Ce-Car@EV NPs with antibacterial activity, the contents of Ce(IV) and Car in the structure were calculated to be 27.2 and 58.4% via inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry analysis. Structurally, protonation of these carboxyl groups under acidic conditions disrupts the metal coordination, triggering structural dissociation and subsequent Car release30. To evaluate the pH-responsive antibiotic release behavior of Ce-Car@EV NPs, we performed in vitro release studies under physiological (pH 7.4) and acidic (pH 5.5) conditions. As shown in Fig. 2f, at pH 5.5, the release efficiency of Car exceeded 70% within 12 h, whereas less than 15% of the antibiotic was released under physiological conditions, demonstrating that the drug release was in a pH-controlled manner. Furthermore, TEM images in Supplementary Fig. 5 reveal the structural disruption of Ce-Car@EV NPs at pH 5.5 over 24 h, along with complete disintegration and disappearance of Ce-Car NCPs within ginger-derived EVs. These results indicate that Ce-Car@EV NPs have the potential for a rapid response to the acidic microenvironment of infection and induce the efficient release of Car, thereby significantly avoiding damage to normal tissues.

Penicillin-binding protein 3 (PBP3) serves as a primary target for various β-lactam antibiotics. By binding to PBP3, Car can effectively inhibit the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall, thereby exerting its antibacterial activity. Notably, the antibacterial efficacy of metal-coordination nanomaterials involves both intact nanoparticles and their degradation products31,32. As Ce-Car@EV NPs degrade in acidic infectious microenvironments, they specifically and targeted release bioactive Ce(IV) and carbenicillin. Therefore, we evaluated the effect of Ce(IV) on the binding mode of Car to PBP3 via molecular docking. As shown in Fig. 2h, in the absence of Ce(IV), Car forms hydrogen bonds with residues Arg483, Asn345, and π–π interactions with Phe401 to produce a binding energy of −6.93 kcal/mol. In the presence of Ce(IV), the binding mode has significantly changed. Ce(IV) forms coordination bonds with the carboxylate group of Glu286 and the backbone oxygen of Arg483, bringing the Car molecule closer to the binding site of Ce(IV). This shift facilitates the formation of additional hydrogen bonds between Car and Tyr524, enhancing the overall binding affinity (Fig. 2i). Meanwhile, the introduction of Ce(IV) reduces the binding energy to −7.84 kcal/mol, suggesting that the electrostatic attraction of Ce(IV) strengthens the interaction between Car and PBP3. These results indicate that Ce(IV) could not only enhance the binding affinity of Car to its target protein but also potentially stabilize the drug-protein complex, thereby augmenting its antibacterial efficacy.

In vitro antibacterial activity and drug resistance studies of Ce-Car@EV NPs
In vitro antibacterial activity of Ce-Car@EV NPs was evaluated using P. aeruginosa as a model bacterium. Considering the distinct microenvironments of normal physiological conditions and infected tissues, the bacterial viability of P. aeruginosa treated by Ce-Car@EV NPs was assessed in vitro under different pH conditions, and the cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay was employed to quantitatively measure the bacterial growth inhibition. At a concentration of 32 μg/mL, the survival rate of bacteria at pH 5.5 was reduced to 3.19%, while the survival rate remained above 80% at pH 7.4 (Fig. 3a). These results clearly demonstrated the significantly enhanced antibacterial activity of Ce-Car@EV NPs in acidic environments, which was attributed to the pH-triggered degradation of Ce-Car@EV NPs and subsequent release of Car. The pH-responsive antibacterial activity of Ce-Car@EV NPs was further verified through a live/dead double staining assay. Under physiological conditions (pH 7.4), P. aeruginosa showed predominantly green fluorescence stained by SYTO-9, associated with living bacteria. In contrast, obvious red fluorescence-associated with dead bacteria was observed under acidic conditions (pH 5.5) in the presence of Ce-Car@EV NPs (Fig. 3b). These results were further supported by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging, which revealed severe structural deformation and membrane disruption of P. aeruginosa treated by Ce-Car@EV NPs at pH 5.5, in contrast to the intact morphology of untreated bacteria (Fig. 3c). To further investigate the interaction between Ce(IV) and Car, the fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was determined using a checkerboard dilution assay. According to the standard classification criteria (FICI ≤ 0.5: synergistic effect; 0.5 < FICI ≤ 1: additive effect; FICI > 1: antagonistic effect), the combination of Ce(IV) and Car exhibited a synergistic effect with FICI of 0.5 (Fig. 3d). These results demonstrate that the two key components of Ce(IV) and Car acted synergistically to enhance antibacterial efficacy.

Continued use of antibiotics can drive the emergence of resistant pathogens. To determine whether the treatment of Ce-Car@EV NPs could induce bacterial resistance comparable to that of free Car, P. aeruginosa was cultured with free Car or Ce-Car@EV NPs at sub-inhibitory concentrations (1/2 MIC) for 30 generations, respectively (Fig. 3e). Under free Car incubation, the 30th-generation MIC increased 256-fold, indicating the rapid development of resistance (designated PA-30R). In contrast, the Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated P. aeruginosa (designated PA-30M) exhibited significantly delayed and a lower degree of resistance. Furthermore, the antibacterial efficacy of Ce-Car@EV NPs against Car-resistant P. aeruginosa (PA-30R) was subsequently assessed, and Fig. 3f revealed that the combination of Ce(IV) and Car maintained a synergistic effect on combating resistant bacteria with a FICI of 0.5. The results of the colony formation assay in Fig. 3g revealed substantial bacterial growth even at free Car up to 2048 μg/mL. In contrast, Ce-Car@EV NPs at 16 μg/mL significantly reduced colony size. Meanwhile, quantitative colony counting demonstrated that the bacterial survival was more than 70% at a Car concentration of 16 μg/mL, while the survival rate dropped to only 0.19% with the treatment of Ce-Car@EV NPs at the equivalent concentration (Fig. 3h, i). These results validate the pH-responsive properties and potent bactericidal capability of Ce-Car@EV NPs due to the synergistic effect between Ce(IV) and Car. Meanwhile, the wide-spectrum antibacterial performance of Ce-Car@EV NPs was also investigated using Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae), another formidable Gram-negative bacterium frequently implicated in pneumonia, as a model. Ce-Car@EV NPs displayed complete bactericidal activity against drug-resistant K. pneumoniae at a concentration of 128 μg/mL following an 8-h co-incubation (Supplementary Fig. 6), which might be attributed to the core antibacterial mechanism, operating through pH-responsive payload release and bacterial energy metabolism disruption. These results indicate the effective elimination of Ce-Car@EV NPs to diverse Gram-negative pathogens, suggesting their considerable potential for applying a wide range of clinically relevant bacterial infections.

Mechanism study of Ce-Car@EV NPs in overcoming drug resistance
To further investigate the underlying mechanisms of Ce-Car@EV NPs to reverse the bacterial resistance, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) transcriptomics was performed on P. aeruginosa, the corresponding PA-30R, and PA-30M. The degree of correlation between gene expression levels in the three experimental groups was reflected by the Pearson correlation coefficient. Significant changes in gene expression levels were observed in PA-30R cells, which may be related to their high antibiotic resistance (Supplementary Fig. 7). The Venn diagram illustrating differences in differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the three groups showed that PA-30R exhibited more DEGs than PA-30M in comparisons with PA (Fig. 4a). Meanwhile, volcano plot analysis revealed that 599 DEGs were upregulated and 126 were downregulated in the group of PA-30M compared to those of PA-30R (Fig. 4b). Compared to the pure P. aeruginosa, 360 DEGs in PA-30R were identified, with 112 upregulated and 248 downregulated genes, while PA-30M showed only 182 DEGs, with 163 upregulated and 19 downregulated types (Fig. 4b). The magnitude of transcriptional alterations in PA-30M relative to pure P. aeruginosa was substantially attenuated compared to that in PA-30R.

Furthermore, gene ontology (GO) analysis in Fig. 4c indicates that DEGs between PA-30M and PA-30R were involved in biological processes (BP), cellular components (CC), and molecular functions (MF). The BP related to the gene expression changes were obviously regulated, including biological regulation, cellular processes, and metabolic processes, et al., while several important CC, such as cellular anatomical entities and protein-containing complexes, were also significantly altered. Additionally, various MF of proteins, such as binding/catalytic activity and transporter activity, exhibited significant changes. The results of GO enrichment analysis reveal that Ce-Car@EV NPs could also affect the bacterial respiratory chain activity and interfere with the bacterial energy metabolism (Supplementary Fig. 8). As shown in Fig. 4d, kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis further identifies key enriched pathways between PA-30M and PA-30R, including carbon metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, pyruvate metabolism, and the citric acid cycle (TCA cycle). Moreover, the comparison of PA-30R and PA-30M with PA revealed that these DEGs were also associated with the metabolic processes, including amino acid metabolism (e.g., the degradation of valine, leucine, and isoleucine, Supplementary Fig. 9). These results indicate that Ce-Car@EV NPs possess the potential to target the regulation of bacterial energy metabolism, including the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.

To reveal the mechanism of Ce-Car@EV NPs participating in bacterial resistance reversal, genes associated with multidrug efflux were analyzed. The heatmap in Fig. 4e shows significant upregulation of major efflux pump genes, including mexA, mexB, oprM, and PA3228 in PA-30R compared with PA. These genes encoded the MexAB-OprM system, a member of the resistance-nodulation-cell-division (RND) superfamily and the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) superfamily, both of which could promote the rapid efflux of Car33,34. In contrast, the expression of these upregulated genes in PA-30M were restored to normal levels or even downregulated, suggesting that Ce-Car@EV NPs could inhibit antibiotic efflux, thereby contributing to the reversal of antibiotic resistance. Beyond inhibiting efflux pump activity, the transcriptomic analysis in Supplementary Fig. 11 also revealed that Ce-Car@EV NPs significantly modulate the expression behaviors of genes associated with biofilm formation, verifying their capacity to disrupt this critical adaptive resistance mechanism, which is frequently responsible for therapeutic tolerance in persistent infections35. Further investigation into bacterial energy metabolism revealed that Ce-Car@EV NPs dramatically reduced the expression level of intracellular ATP, a vital energy source for cells, which was closely linked to oxidative phosphorylation and the electron transport chain. As shown in Fig. 4f, genes encoding complex I (nuoE, nuoG, nuoI, nuoN) and IV (ccoN2, coxB, cyoD) were significantly downregulated in the PA-30M group. This downregulation directly leads to proton motive force (PMF) dissipation36,37, indicating that Ce(IV) has the capacity to interfere with the bacterial respiration. Additionally, genes involving in the glycolysis and TCA cycle, such as pyruvate kinase (pykA), α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (sucB), and aconitase (acnA), were downregulated, suggesting the suppression of bacterial energy metabolism induced by treatment of Ce-Car@EV NPs (Fig. 4g). Meanwhile, the expression levels of genes closely related to P. aeruginosa virulence are also shown in the heatmap (Supplementary Fig. 10), indicating that most of the genes encoding pathogenesis-associated toxins were down-regulated. Collectively, these multi-faceted transcriptional alterations- spanning virulence attenuation, energy metabolism disruption, efflux pump suppression, and biofilm formation inhibition- converge into a unified resistance-reversal mechanism, thereby significantly enhancing the potential to combat complex resistance profiles in P. aeruginosa. Figure 4h provides a detailed summary of the mechanism by which Ce-Car@EV NPs overcome P. aeruginosa resistance. After the treatment of Ce-Car@EV NPs, the bacterial glycolysis was severely inhibited, as evidenced by the significant down-regulated expression of genes related to the conversion between glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and glycerate-3-phosphate in this pathway. In addition, genes associated with aconitase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and succinyl-CoA synthetase were also significantly down-regulated in the TCA cycle. Critically, this metabolic perturbation extends to compensatory pathways, evidenced by genes associated with the synthesis and metabolism of glyoxylate were also down-regulated, a key anaplerotic circuit that bypasses decarboxylation steps in the TCA cycle38,39. The resultant energy crisis is further amplified by the Ce(IV)-mediated down-regulation of respiratory complex I and complex IV genes, which directly dissipates PMF. Furthermore, the respiratory chain activities of complex I and complex IV were also significantly reduced in Car-resistant P. aeruginosa after Ce-Car@EV NPs treatment, confirming that Ce(IV) could disrupt bacterial energy metabolism and prevent the operation of energy-dependent efflux pumps (Fig. 4k). ATP hydrolysis assay in Fig. 4i demonstrates that Ce-Car@EV NPs could greatly decrease the content of intracellular ATP in a concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 4j), achieving a 60% reduction at 100 μg/mL and revealing their strong potential to effectively deplete bacterial ATP. To functionally assess inhibition capacity to the efflux pump, ethidium bromide (EtBr), a well-characterized fluorescent substrate for RND-type efflux pumps in P. aeruginosa, was utilized to verify the impaired pump activity via direct monitoring of intracellular fluorescence accumulation40,41. Fig. 4l demonstrates that Ce-Car@EV NPs significantly inhibited the efflux pump activity in a concentration-dependent manner, further reinforcing their role in reversing bacterial resistance by blocking the energy supply for efflux pumps. By coordinately normalizing efflux pump transcription, disrupting energy metabolism, and functionally compromising efflux pumps, Ce-Car@EV NPs establishes a powerful multi-mode mechanism that reverses carbenicillin resistance of drug-resistant bacteria at both transcriptional and functional levels.

Biocompatibility of Ce-Car@EV NPs in vitro and in vivo
The potential toxicity and biocompatibility assessment of biomaterials is of paramount importance to ensure their feasibility for clinical and biomedical applications. Therefore, the cytotoxicity and hemolytic activity of Ce-Car@EV NPs were systematically evaluated. The cytotoxicity of Ce-Car@EV NPs was systematically evaluated using three representative cell types, including mouse fibroblast L929, murine macrophage RAW264.7, and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Cell viability in all three lineages remained above 80% even after 24 h of co-culture with Ce-Car@EV NPs at a concentration of 512 μg/mL, indicating negligible cytotoxicity (Supplementary Fig. 12a–c). Additionally, the hemolytic activity of Ce-Car@EV NPs was measured using mouse red blood cells (RBCs). When the extracted RBCs were incubated with 512 μg/mL of Ce-Car@EV NPs for 3 h, the hemolysis ratio was less than 5%, demonstrating the favorable hemocompatibility of Ce-Car@EV NPs (Supplementary Fig. 12d). Furthermore, the in vivo biocompatibility of Ce-Car@EV NPs was examined. Mice injected intravenously with Ce-Car@EV NPs displayed a weight gain trajectory similar to that of untreated control mice over 7 days, along with stable body temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 13), indicating negligible adverse effects of Ce-Car@EV NPs on mouse growth. Meanwhile, routine blood tests and serum biochemical analyses showed no significant differences between Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated and healthy mice (Supplementary Fig. 14). Histopathological examination of major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys, and brain, revealed negligible pathological abnormalities after the injection of Ce-Car@EV NPs compared to controls after 7 days (Supplementary Fig. 15). Oxidative stress is recognized as a primary concern contributing to nanoparticle-induced neurotoxicity42,43. To assess the potential neurotoxic effects of Ce-Car@EV NPs, several key oxidative stress markers in the mouse central nervous system, including superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione (GSH), and malondialdehyde (MDA), were examined. After 7 days of treatment with Ce-Car@EV NPs, the cerebral cortex showed insignificant alterations in the levels of SOD, GSH, or MDA relative to the control group (Supplementary Fig. 16). These results suggest that Ce-Car@EV NPs administration provoke negligible substantial oxidative injury within neural tissues. These results demonstrate that Ce-Car@EV NPs displayed favorable biocompatibility and minimal biotoxicity both in vitro and in vivo, underscoring their potential as a safe and effective therapeutic platform for bacterial infections.

In vivo pharmacokinetics, biodistribution and metabolism of Ce-Car@EV NPs
The robust in vitro antimicrobial capacity and good biocompatibility of Ce-Car@EV NPs suggest their potential for combating bacterial infections in vivo. After intravenous injection, numerous studies demonstrate that natural EV camouflage can extend the blood circulation time and enhance preferential accumulation of nanomaterials at the infection sites44. To validate the extended blood circulation capability conferred by G-EVs coating, we compared the cellular uptake of Ce-Car NCPs and Ce-Car@EV NPs by RAW264.7 macrophages in vitro. Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) images confirmed that the rational encapsulation of G-EVs significantly reduced the phagocytosis of Ce-Car@EV NPs compared to the bare Ce-Car NCPs (Supplementary Fig. 17). This diminished immunocellular clearance capacity is crucial for prolonging the systemic circulation of the nanoplatform. Upon reaching the pulmonary vasculature, most of the traditional nanoparticles initially accumulate through the EPR effect resulting from infection-induced vascular hyperpermeability45,46. Furthermore, this targeted enhanced accumulation is augmented by the complementary biological mechanisms. The infected pulmonary microenvironment typically exhibits substantial infiltration of M1-polarized macrophages, demonstrating heightened phagocytic activity toward nano-sized structures. Additionally, tremendous studies on plant-derived EVs document their inherent targeted capability to the inflammatory site, including the potential affinity toward M1 macrophages47,48. These coordinated mechanisms, including prolonged circulation, passive EPR-mediated accumulation, and potential active targeted processes, may collectively contribute to the enhanced targeting efficacy of Ce-Car@EV NPs. To validate these properties, Cy7-labeled Ce-Car@EV NPs were intravenously administered to mice with drug-resistant P. aeruginosa-infected lungs, and their biodistribution was tracked at various time points using fluorescence imaging (Fig. 5a). As shown in Fig. 5b, Cy7-related fluorescence signals in mice injected with bare Ce-Car NCPs were predominantly localized in the liver, with minimal accumulation in the infected lung. These fluorescence signals obviously diminished after 8 h, probably due to the rapid immune clearance. In contrast, mice with lung infections treated with Ce-Car@EV NPs exhibited significantly stronger and more sustained fluorescence signals in the infected lung, indicating enhanced and prolonged retention. Quantitative fluorescence analysis demonstrates that Ce-Car@EV NPs began accumulating in the infected lungs within 2 h post-injection, and peaked at 6 h, with significantly higher accumulation than bare Ce-Car NCPs (Fig. 5c). These findings were further confirmed by fluorescence imaging and quantitative analysis of isolated organs at 6 h post-injection, demonstrating the efficient and selective accumulation of Ce-Car@EV NPs in infected lungs, along with the prolonged retention (Fig. 5d, e). Interestingly, the targeted accumulation of Ce-Car@EV NPs depending on the specific pathological microenvironment of bacterial infection was unequivocally verified through control experiments in healthy mice. The intravenous administration of Ce-Car@EV NPs in healthy mice resulted in negligible pulmonary fluorescence signals, exhibiting a stark contrast with the substantial accumulation in the lungs of pneumonic mice (Supplementary Fig. 18). These results demonstrate that the targeted efficiency of Ce-Car@EV NPs is intrinsically associated with the inflammatory microenvironment, rather than the nonspecific distribution. Taken together, these results suggest that the biomimetic camouflage with ginger-derived EVs effectively promotes the targeted delivery of Ce-Car@EV NPs to bacterial infection sites.

To quantitatively track the in vivo trajectory of Ce-Car@EV NPs, we systematically investigated its pharmacokinetic profile and metabolic fate. Following the intravenous administration of Ce-Car@EV NPs in healthy mice, blood samples were collected at predetermined time points and subjected to quantitative analysis of cerium ions. Pharmacokinetic data via a non-compartmental model determined the circulating half-life of Ce-Car@EV NPs to be 6.68 h (Fig. 5f), providing a critical kinetic foundation for the enhanced accumulation at the infection site. Meanwhile, the excretory pathways of the nanoplatform were traced by monitoring cerium levels in urine and feces. As summarized in Fig. 5g, h, Ce-Car@EV NPs underwent dual clearance routes involving hepatic metabolism and renal excretion, showing a near-complete elimination within 7 days, which was consistent to the quantification of residual cerium in major organs with only minimal retention (Supplementary Fig. 19). These results indicate a good pharmacokinetic profile characterized by extended circulation, defined clearance mechanisms, and negligible long-term organ accumulation. This profile affirms the robust biodegradability and biosafety of Ce-Car@EV NPs, underscoring their potential as a translatable antimicrobial agent.

In vivo therapeutic performance of Ce-Car@EV NPs for P. aeruginosa-induced lung infection
Encouraged by the potent antibacterial properties, good biosafety, and efficient targeted accumulation at the infection sites, the in vivo antimicrobial efficacy of Ce-Car@EV nanoplatforms was assessed using drug-resistant P. aeruginosa-infected lung model in mice. Commercial mice were intratracheally inoculated with 50 μL of drug-resistant P. aeruginosa, and neutrophil reduction was induced by cyclophosphamide. Two hours post-infection, the infected mice were randomly divided into four groups and respectively treated with the intravenous injections of saline (control), free Car, Ce-Car NCPs, and Ce-Car@EV NPs (Fig. 6a), while untreated mice served as the healthy group. Survival rates were monitored over 36-h, alongside physiological measurements of body temperatures and body weight. As shown in Fig. 6b, all infected mice treated with saline, Car, or Ce-Car NCPs died within 36 h, whereas those injected with Ce-Car@EV NPs exhibited a satisfactory survival rate, indicating their therapeutic potential against P. aeruginosa lung infection. Additionally, the body temperatures and weight of Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice remained stable, comparable to healthy controls, suggesting negligible side effects (Fig. 6c, d). Clinical scores on six typical parameters, including activity, coat condition, eyes, breathing, posture, and isolation, were also significantly improved in the Ce-Car@EV NPs group (Fig. 6f). These results indicate that Ce-Car@EV NPs are highly effective against acute lung infections when administered intravenously, without adverse effects on mouse health.

Furthermore, lungs from mice receiving different treatments were collected and analyzed at 12 and 60 h post-treatment. As shown in Fig. 6e, visual inspection of the lung tissues revealed clear differences in treatment efficacy between the Ce-Car@EV NPs group and other groups. After the treatment of saline, Car, or Ce-Car NCPs, the lung tissues were red and mottled, exhibiting congestion and focal infections. In contrast, lungs from Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice appeared pink with fewer focal infections, demonstrating effective treatment of P. aeruginosa infection. Quantification of residual bacteria in lung homogenates and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) further confirmed the antibacterial efficacy of Ce-Car@EV NPs. As shown in Fig. 6g and Supplementary Fig. 20a, bacterial counts in Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated lungs decreased by over two orders of magnitude versus the other groups, with the lowest bacterial counts observed in BALF (Fig. 6h and Supplementary Fig. 20b). At 60 h post-treatment, bacterial load in both lung homogenates and BALF of the Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice decreased by one order of magnitude compared to those at 12 h post-treatment (Supplementary Fig. 21). In contrast, saline, Car, or bare Ce-Car NCPs-treated mice showed bacterial spread to heart, liver, spleen, and kidneys at 12 h post-treatment, indicating systemic infection. Throughout treatment, Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice maintained minimal bacterial loads in all major organs (Supplementary Fig. 22). Notably, by the 60 h post-treatment time point, Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice showed further reductions or undetectable bacterial loads in all major organs compared to the 12 h post-treatment time point (Supplementary Fig. 23), demonstrating the great potential for targeted antibacterial treatment of the infected lung. Fluorescence images of P. aeruginosa-stained lung sections confirmed obviously lower bacterial loads in Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated lungs compared with other groups (Fig. 6i). These results demonstrate that Ce-Car@EV NPs effectively inactivated drug-resistant P. aeruginosa in both infected lungs and distant organs, establishing their therapeutic potential for the treatment of multidrug-resistant bacterial infections.

The lung wet-to-dry (W/D) ratio, a well-established indicator of pulmonary edema, was measured to evaluate the extent of lung tissue damage, specifically assessing the influx of protein-rich edema fluid into alveolar spaces caused by increased capillary-endothelial-alveolar epithelial barrier permeability49. As shown in Fig. 7a, the control group exhibited the highest lung W/D ratio, indicating significant pulmonary edema. In contrast, the W/D ratio of the lung treated by Ce-Car@EV NPs was significantly lower than those in the Car and Ce-Car NCPs groups, suggesting that Ce-Car@EV NPs treatment effectively alleviated lung edema. Further analysis of the total protein concentration and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity in BALF revealed that Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated lungs displayed low levels of edema fluid and minimal tissue damage (Fig. 7b, c). Additionally, the assessment of lung lesion severity using the lung index was consistent with these findings, showing an obvious reduction in lesion extents in Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice (Fig. 7d). Taken together, these results demonstrate that Ce-Car@EV NPs could effectively inhibit the influx of protein-rich edema fluid into the alveoli, mitigate lung injury, and reduce mortality in bacterially infected mice.

Moreover, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and Masson staining were employed to evaluate the pathological changes in lung sections following different treatments. As shown in Fig. 7e, H&E staining images revealed noticeable inflammatory cell infiltration in the control group, along alveolar septum thickening, alveolar wall changes, and partial alveolar shrinkage, as well as extensive regional consolidation. In contrast, histological lesions in Car- and Ce-Car NCPs-treated mice were alleviated to some extent, though significant abnormalities persisted. Notably, lung tissues from Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice exhibited nearly normal structures. Masson staining in Fig. 7f further verified these observations, showing the relatively intact alveolar structures and minimal fibrosis in Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated mice, whereas other treatment groups showed pronounced lung fibrosis changes. Collectively, these results demonstrate that Ce-Car@EV NPs significantly enhanced the in vivo antibacterial efficacy of Car and provided significantly therapeutic benefits for acute lung infections, facilitating the recovery of lung structure and function.

## Methods

Materials and reagents
Ceric ammonium nitrate, sucrose, and cyclophosphamide monohydrate were purchased from Energy Chemical (Shanghai, China). Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP, MW=55000), ethidium bromide and 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2yl)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazolium bromide (MTT) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich Chemical Co. (St Louis, MO, USA). Dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO, >90%) and ethanol (>99.7%) were provided by Beijing Chemical Works (China). Cyanine7 amine (Cy7-NH2) and carbenicillin disodium were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co. (China). Glutaraldehyde (GA) was obtained from Sinopharm Group Co., Ltd (China). The LIVE/DEAD BacLight Bacterial Viability Kit (L7012) was purchased from Invitrogen (Life-Technologies, USA). Anti-Pseudomonas outer membrane porin F antibody (Abcam, catalog no. ab316973, clone: EPR28629-91) and CD9 rabbit pAb (Bioss, catalog no. bs-2489R) were obtained from the respective manufacturers and used at dilutions of 1:100 and 1:500, respectively. The lysogeny broth (LB) solution was autoclaved for 20 min at 120 °C before use. The strains of P. aeruginosa (ATCC 27853) was provided by Promega (Madison, USA). The drug-resistant K. pneumoniae strain was a clinical isolate obtained from the Chinese PLA General Hospital. Milli-Q Ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ) was used in all experiments unless otherwise stated.

Isolation and purification of ginger-derived extracellular vesicles (G-EVs)
G-EVs were extracted from fresh ginger according to the previous literatures52,53. Fresh ginger was purchased from a local shop and washed repeatedly with deionized water and saline. Ginger was cut into small pieces, ground in a juicer, and immersed in saline to collect the juice. Ginger outer membrane vesicles were first coarsely extracted by differential centrifugation at 200 × g for 10 min, 2000 × g for 20 min, and 10,000 × g for 30 min to remove large particles as well as precipitated cells and debris. The supernatant was collected and centrifuged at 150,000 × g in an ultracentrifuge for 2 h. The precipitate was collected and resuspended in saline. Ginger outer membrane vesicles were further purified by sucrose gradient centrifugation, and the precipitate resuspended in saline was transferred to a sucrose gradient (8%, 20%, 30%, 45%) and centrifuged at 150,000 × g for 2 h. Ginger outer membrane vesicles were finally floated in different sucrose bands. All the processes were carried out at 4 °C. The bands between 8/30 and 30/45% were collected separately and washed with saline. Finally, the precipitates were taken by centrifugation at 150,000 × g for 1 h and resuspended in saline, quantified by the BCA protein quantification kit, and stored at −80 °C for backup.

Synthesis of Ce-Car@EV NPs
Briefly, Ce(NH4)2(NO3)6 (16.272 mg) and PVP (48.816 mg) were mixed in a glass vial containing 3 mL of deionized water. The mixture was stirred at 700 rpm for 2 h at room temperature to obtain a homogeneous light-yellow solution. Subsequently, carbenicillin sodium (15.204 mg) was added dropwise to the light-yellow solution, and the mixed solution was stirred for another 10 min to obtain a final light-yellow suspension. The light-yellow suspension was centrifuged at 20,000 rpm for 30 min, washed three times and resuspended in deionized water to obtain Ce-Car NCPs. Subsequently, the prepared Ce-Car NCPs were transferred to a centrifuge tube, and 6 mg of purified ginger-derived EVs were added and sonicated in an ice bath. Finally, the product was incubated at 37 °C for 1 h and then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 30 min, collected and resuspended in saline to obtain Ce-Car@EV NPs.

Checkerboard analysis and FIC index determination
Synergistic interaction between Ce(IV) and Car was assessed by checkerboard analysis. Briefly, the solution containing Ce(IV) and Car was placed in 96-well plates at 2-fold serial dilution to form an 8 × 8 matrix. The final volume of each well was 150 μL containing 1 × 105 CFU/mL bacteria. After 24 h of incubation at 37 °C on a shaker, the absorbance value at 600 nm of each well was determined. The synergistic effect of Ce(IV) and Car was evaluated by calculating the FIC index. The calculation formula was presented as follows.

FIC index = FICA + FICB (1)

where FICA was the MIC of Ce(IV) in combination/MIC of Ce(IV) alone, and FICB was the MIC of Car in combination/MIC of Car alone.

Resistance studies
Changes in resistance of P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853 were investigated by sequential passaging assay under sub-MIC conditions of sequential exposure to Car and Ce-Car@EV NPs according to the previous literature54. Firstly, MIC of Car and Ce-Car@EV NPs were determined via a microbroth dilution assay. For subsequent passages, 1 × 105 CFU/mL of bacteria were inoculated into medium containing serial dilutions of Car or Ce-Car@EV NPs, and passages were performed at 24-h intervals. The absorbance values at 600 nm were measured by a microplate detector to determine the MIC of the bacteria after different treatments. Bacteria co-cultured with 1/2 MIC value of each group was used for passaging, and the above steps were repeated for 30 days. The MIC of each passage was recorded and compared with that of the first passage. Under the same culture protocol, a distinct carbenicillin-resistant strain (PA-15R) was generated through 15 sequential passages of the parental ATCC 27853 strain in the standard and undiluted LB medium containing carbenicillin, which was utilized for subsequent antibacterial efficacy evaluation.

Bactericidal properties of Ce-Car@EV NPs
In vitro antimicrobial activity of Ce-Car@EV NPs was systematically assessed by CCK-8 assay, CLSM, SEM and standard plate counting method. Firstly, the bacteria were inoculated into LB culture medium on a shaker at 37 °C overnight and cultured to logarithmic phase. The antibacterial assays were performed in 10 mM tris-HCl buffer at two distinct pH values (5.5 and 7.4), with the pH carefully adjusted using hydrochloric acid. Diluted log-phase bacteria (8 × 106 CFU/mL) were treated with Ce-Car@EV NPs (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 μg/mL) dispersed in the respective buffers. After 2 h of co-culture, bacterial viability of each group was calculated using the CCK-8 method.

Furthermore, CLSM images were employed to visually observe the antibacterial effect of Ce-Car@EV NPs under different pH conditions using the live/dead double staining method. Bacterial suspensions (108 CFU/mL) were dispersed in the buffers containing Ce-Car@EV NPs (512 μg/mL) under different pH conditions (5.5 or 7.4) and co-cultivated for 6 h. Bacterial suspensions receiving different treatments were centrifuged, washed, and collected. The bacterial suspension (109 CFU/mL) was then double-stained with a mixture of SYTO-9/PI and maintained in the dark for 15 min. Then, the stained bacteria were observed by CLSM, and the bacteria treated by PBS were regarded as controls. Finally, the morphology of bacteria after different treatments were also characterized by SEM imaging.

Antimicrobial effect of Ce-Car@EV NPs under different experimental conditions were further quantified by the standard plate counting method. Bacterial suspensions (105 CFU/mL) were respectively treated by Car or Ce-Car@EV NPs at different concentrations (0, 2, 4, 8, and 16 μg/mL) for 4 h, and aliquots were taken out of the suspensions and serially diluted. Then, 50 μL of diluted bacterial suspensions from each group were inoculated onto LB agar plates, and the bacterial survival rates were counted and calculated after 18 h of incubation.

In vivo biodistribution of Ce-Car@EV NPs
Female Balb/c mice (8 weeks old), an inbred strain, were acquired from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co. (China) and housed with a 12 h light/dark cycle under controlled ambient temperature (22 °C) and humidity (30–70%). Given the anticipated applicability of findings to both sexes, and that gender was not a study variable, female mice were selected to align with standard models. In vivo biodistribution of Ce-Car@EV NPs was evaluated using in vivo fluorescent imaging. The mice were fasted overnight prior to the experiment, and the chests and abdomens of the mice were exposed. After the mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, 50 μL of drug-resistant P. aeruginosa (7 × 107 CFU/mL) was injected into the lungs of healthy mice via the trachea to establish a mouse model of acute pneumonia induced by drug-resistant P. aeruginosa. After 2 h, drug-resistant P. aeruginosa-infected mice were randomly divided into two groups (n = 3) and intravenously injected with 100 μL of Cy7-labeled Ce-Car NCPs and Cy7-labeled Ce-Car@EV NPs (the concentration of Ce-Car NCPs was 4 mg/mL), respectively. Fluorescence images of mouse lungs were acquired at predetermined time points (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 24 h) post-injection by the Xenogen IVIS spectrum imaging system (Caliper Life Sciences, America). To further assess the distribution of nanoparticles in isolated organs, mice were sacrificed 6 h post-administration and major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys) were collected for fluorescence imaging. The fluorescence signals from these major organs were qualitatively observed and quantitatively analyzed.

Establishment of mouse lung infection model
Neutropenia and granulocytopenia were induced in mice by administering 150 and 100 mg/kg of cyclophosphamide 4 days prior to infection and 1 day prior to infection, respectively55. Bacterial lung infections were induced by anesthetizing mice with isoflurane, removing hair from the backs of the mice, and intratracheal nebulized inoculation of mice with drug-resistant P. aeruginosa (50 μL, 5 × 107 CFU/mL). Two hours post-infection, the infected mice were randomly divided into four experimental groups (n = 5), with healthy mice serving as the negative control. The mice received intravenous injection with 100 μL of saline, Car (carbenicillin concentration = 1.168 mg/mL), Ce-Car NCPs (containing Car = 1.168 mg/mL), and Ce-Car@EV NPs (containing Car = 1.168 mg/mL), respectively. Treatments were administered every 12 h for a total of three times. Animal temperature and body weight were monitored every 2 h for survival studies. A portion of mice was sacrificed 12 and 60 h after different treatments, and pre-cooled sterile saline (1 mL) was slowly injected from the trachea. BALF was collected by repeatedly aspirating the lung solution three times to ensure that the recovery of BALF was greater than 80%. The BALF was further tested for bacterial enumeration using the standard plate counting method. The remaining BALF was then centrifuged, and the total protein concentration in BALF was determined using a BCA protein assay kit, and the LDH concentration in the lung lavage fluid was determined using an LDH assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute). Lung tissues were photographed and accurately weighed on an electronic balance, which was defined as the wet weight, and then dried in an oven at 65 °C for 72 h until the weight did not change, which was defined as the dry weight, to calculate the wet/dry (W/D) ratio of the lungs. Mouse lung tissues and major organ samples (heart, liver, spleen, and kidney) after different treatments were collected, homogenized and diluted in plates to determine the colony counts. Then, the bacterial load in the lungs of infected mice was quantified as the total number of bacteria in the lung homogenates and BALF.

Lung histology and immunofluorescence staining
The collected lungs were fixed in 4% tissue fixative for over 24 h. Then, the lungs were embedded in paraffin, cut into thin slices, stained with H&E and Masson, and visualized by microscopy. For immunofluorescence detection of P. aeruginosa, lung sections were stained with primary antibody (anti-P. aeruginosa antibody, Abcam, act. no. ab316973) and fluorescently labeled secondary antibody according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All sections were finally stained with DAPI and imaged using a CLSM.

Clinical scores of mice
Mice were scored in six categories, including fur, activity, eyes, respiration, posture, and isolation, with scores of 0, 1, and 2 for each category, containing (A) coat (0, no fur erection; 1, slight fur erection; 2, significant fur erection), (B) activity (0, mice displaying normal levels of activity including exploratory behaviors and locomotion; 1, slightly reduced activity, but still responding to stimuli; 2, markedly reduced activity and reduced response to stimuli), (C) eyes (0, clear, bright eyes with no discharge; 1, slight periocular discharge or slight eyelid swelling; 2, marked periocular discharge, eyes half-closed), (D) breathing (0, normal, even rhythmic respiration; 1, slight increase in respiratory rate or slight abnormal respiration; 2, marked respiratory distress, such as nasal flaring, shoulder movement), (E) posture (0, normal, with limbs supporting the body and no abnormal postures; 1, obvious postural irregularities, such as hunching, or squatting most of the time; 2, abnormal postures, such as reclining, inability to stand properly), and (F) isolation (0, normal social interactions, including interaction and playfulness with peers; 1, slight decrease in socialization, and will still engage in some peer interaction; 2, obvious isolating behavior, often avoiding peer interaction).

Biosafety of Ce-Car@EV NPs
Briefly, healthy mice were randomly divided into two groups (n = 3), and the hair on the back of the mice was shaved. Ce-Car@EV NPs (100 μL, 4 mg/mL) were injected intravenously, and the untreated healthy mice were employed as controls. The body temperature and body weight of the animals were monitored once a day. After 7 days, the major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and brain) of mice were collected for H&E staining. For blood biochemical analysis, expression levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine (CREA) were determined. In the complete blood count test, contents of white blood cells (WBC), RBC, neutrophil (Neut), lymphocyte (Lymph), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), and erythrocyte corpuscle (HCT) were determined.

Evaluation of cytotoxicity in vitro
L929 cells were inoculated into 96-well plates at a cell density of 1 × 104/well and cultured in an incubator containing 5% CO2 at 37 °C for 24 h. Subsequently, Ce-Car@EV NPs at different concentrations (8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 μg/mL) were co-cultured with L929 cells. After 24 h the medium was removed, and the prepared MTT solution (100 μL, 0.5 mg/mL) was added, and further incubated at 37 °C for 4 h. Finally, the medium was removed, and 100 μL of DMSO was added to each well and shaken at low speed for 10 min. The absorbance value of each well at 490 nm was measured and recorded by a microplate detector.

Blood was collected from Balb/c mice receiving different treatments, and then centrifuged at 4 °C for 15 min to obtain precipitated RBCs. The erythrocytes were rinsed with saline to make the supernatant colorless, and the erythrocyte suspension was diluted to 4% v/v with saline. The erythrocyte suspension was co-incubated with Ce-Car@EV NPs at different concentrations (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 μg/mL) for 3 h at 37 °C. Saline and Triton-X were used as a negative and positive control, respectively. Then, the mixture of erythrocytes and Ce-Car@EV NPs was centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 15 min. Finally, the absorbance value of the supernatant at 540 nm were recorded using a microplate detector and the percentage of hemolysis was calculated. The formula for calculating the percentage of hemolysis is presented as follows.

Hemolysis (%) = (ODM − ODN) / (ODP − ODN) × 100% (2)

Where ODM, ODP, and ODN present the absorbance values of Ce-Car@EV NPs-treated groups, positive control group and negative control group, respectively.

Statistical analysis
Data were presented as means ± standard deviation and are from at least three independent experiments. The differences were calculated by using two-tailed Student’s t test for two groups or one-way ANOVA for three or more groups. The statistical analysis were carried out with the software of Excel 2019 or GraphPad Prism. The level of significance in all statistical analyses was set at P < 0.05.

### Reviewer 1

Ye and colleagues introduce Ce-Car@EV, a nanoparticle made from a cerium-carbenicillin complex and ginger-derived
vesicles, emphasizing its potential for treating bacterial pneumonia. This nanoparticle demonstrates effective bactericidal
properties and in vitro/in vivo biocompatibility, targeting the lungs via the EPR effect to combat Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
The study is well-structured, including antibacterial experiments against drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa,
construction and sequencing of drug-resistant strains, and an exploration of bacterial resistance mechanisms. However, the
study focuses solely on Pseudomonas aeruginosa, raising concerns about its broad-spectrum antibacterial efficacy. The
antibacterial effectiveness against other key pathogens causing bacterial pneumonia, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae
and Klebsiella pneumoniae, remains unexplored, limiting its clinical applicability. Additionally, the mechanism by which
ginger vesicles, as an external substance, extend their time in the bloodstream is not fully addressed. While the combination
of cerium-based nanoparticles and ginger vesicles is innovative, the research lacks significant innovation in material
synthesis and mechanism exploration. The study does not provide groundbreaking insights into material preparation or
biomedical issues. Given the innovative nature of the topic and the experimental data, it is challenging to meet the standards
of Nature Communications. It is recommended to either reject the paper or submit it to Communications Materials.
1. Given that this paper builds on your lab's prior research, the choice of ginger-derived vesicles is understandable.
However, it seems counterintuitive to claim that these vesicles, as exogenous substances, can evade the immune system.
Compared to mammalian cells, ginger vesicles and other plant vesicles, as foreign entities, are more likely to be recognized
and engulfed by immune cells, potentially affecting their effectiveness. The authors should conduct relevant experiments
and provide reliable data to support this claim, such as immune cell phagocytosis assays or bacterial phagocytosis assays.
Additionally, considering the recent extensive studies on natural product-derived vesicles, most of which are believed to
have immunomodulatory properties, it would be valuable to investigate whether the ginger-derived vesicles used in this
paper have other effects during the treatment of bacterial infections. Additionally, offer reasonable justifications for selecting
ginger vesicles over vesicles from other plants.
2. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains used in both in vitro and in vivo experiments should be clearly specified. According

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a highly innovative and well-executed study on the development and evaluation of a biomimetic
nanoplatform (Ce-Car@EV) for combating drug-resistant P. aeruginosa. The work addresses the critical global challenge of
antimicrobial resistance (AMR) through a sophisticated strategy combining pH-responsive metal-drug coordination
nanoparticles (i.e. Ce-Car NPs) with ginger-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs). Extensive physicochemical
characterization (TEM, XPS, FTIR, zeta potential, SDS-PAGE) confirmed successful synthesis, EV coating, and pH-
responsive degradation. Transcriptomics (RNA-seq) and pathway analysis (KEGG/GO) convincingly demonstrated
downregulation of efflux pumps (mexAB-oprM), oxidative phosphorylation, and TCA cycle genes, linking Ce(IV) to energy
disruption. The nanoplatform significantly improves survival, reduces bacterial loads in lungs/organs, alleviates lung injury,
and demonstrates targeted accumulation via EV-mediated evasion of immune clearance. However, these authors need to
address the following issues:
1. Safety of Ce(IV): While biocompatibility is shown, long-term biodistribution/accumulation of cerium in organs should be
addressed (e.g., via ICP-MS in tissues beyond 7 days, selectivity between bacterial cells and mammalian cells).
2. Direct evidence such as efflux assay with fluorescent substrates like Hoechst 33342 to complement transcriptomic data,
shall be added.
3. Figure 2C: It should be “LUMO” instead of “HUMO”
4. Line 215-219: “According to the standard classification criteria (FICI ≤0.5: synergistic effect; 0.5 < FICI ≤ 1: additive effect;
FICI > 1: no interaction), the combination of Ce(IV) and Car exhibited a strong synergistic effect with FICI of 0.5.” According
to your description, FICI 0.5 can not be defined as “Strong synergistic effect”, and it should be additive effect between your
two drugs. This exaggeration occurs many times and describes the mechanism reluctantly. Also, FICI>1 should be
antagonistic effect instead of no interaction.
5. Figure 3a and 3f, the bacterial viability of Ce-Car@EV seems not constant. Why resistant strains even demonstrated lower
bacterial viability (0%) under the treatment of 16 μg/ml CE-Car@EV compared with sensitive strains (20%). Please clarify
the bacterial strains used in each figure in figure captions.
6. The Ce-Car@EV platform combines innovative design, mechanistic rigor, and compelling in vivo validation, however, the
synergistic effect seems reluctant and overall the mechanism is confusing. These authors shall clarify it.
7. These authors presented the use of Ce-Car@EV nanoplatform for AMR. However, in the docking simulation, they use Car
and Ce(IV) ions. They shall address the gap between nano materials and small molecules and ions (metabolism and/or
decomposition). Key references shall be cited: Nat Rev Chem. 2023,7, 202-224; J. Am Chem Soc. 2025, 147, 12361-12380.

### Reviewer 3

In this work, Ye et al. developed ginger-derived extracellular vesicle (EV)-encapsulated cerium-carbenicillin nanoplatforms
(Ce-Car@EV) with the antibacterial capacity by the disruption of bacterial energy metabolism. The nanoplatform utilizes the
Ce⁴⁺ ions to induce ATP depletion and proton motive force dissipation to reverse efflux pump-driven resistance, which can
significantly enhance carbenicillin efficacy against drug-resistant P. aeruginosa. Experimental results in vivo demonstrate
the reduced bacterial burden and improved survival in a murine pneumonia model. However, there are still some issues in
the manuscript that need to be addressed. Therefore, I think this article is worthy of being published in Nature
Communications after minor revisions.
1. The biological role of G-EVs as drug carriers requires more detailed biochemical validation. Current characterizations via
TEM and SDS-PAGE cannot fully confirm their exosomal properties. Western blotting analysis should be performed to
assess conserved exosome markers and verify vesicle integrity.
2. Compared with mammalian cell-derived EVs, plant-derived edible EVs exhibit lower immunogenicity, along with
advantages in sustainability and renewability. The yield of ginger-derived exosomes requires quantification.
3. The cytotoxicity assessment in murine fibroblasts provides preliminary evidence of biocompatibility; however, evaluation
across additional cell lines is needed to obtain a comprehensive safety profile.
4. Although Supplementary Figures 9-11 confirm systemic biocompatibility at therapeutic concentrations in vivo, the
potential neurotoxicity of cerium ions requires specific evaluation in neural tissues.
5. Several graphical elements require clarification. Specifically, in Fig. 2c, the label 'HUMO' should be corrected to 'LUMO'
(lowest unoccupied molecular orbital) to ensure accurate representation of molecular orbitals.
6. Reference formatting requires consistent verification. For example, the volume and page numbers for Reference No. 5
should be provided.
